newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian accused reject subversion charges.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian accused reject subversion charges.

text.p: Two leading Indonesian activists on trial for subversion and spreading hatred against the government rejected the charges on Thursday, saying they had acted within the law.

In the Central Jakarta State Court, Budiman Sudjatmiko, chairman of the left-wing People's Democratic Party (PRD), told the court that everything he had done was open and in accordance with the country's constitution.

In the South Jakarta State Court, independent labour activist Muchtar Pakpahan said he was being charged under laws that were out-of-date as they orginated in Dutch colonial times or before President Suharto's 30-year New Order government.
Sudjatmiko said the government had blamed his group for the July 27 riots in Jakarta, regarded as the worst in more than 20 years, to divert guilt away from itself.

After the government used the riots to arrest a number of PRD members and Pakpahan days after the event, none of the charges directly link the accused to the riots, in which at least five people died.

"Clean water, if you keep stirring it, becomes murky. Especially when the hand doing the stirring is dirty and trying to wash itself clean," Sudjatmiko told the court in his reply to the indictment read last week at the trial opening.

Nine members of the PRD, including Sudjatmiko, are concurrently facing the same charges in five trials in two courts after they were accused of trying to overthrow the government as the PRD did not follow the state ideology Pancasila.
"We have argued there was no criminal aspects to his conduct," one of Sudjatmiko's defence lawyers, Luhut Pangaribuan, said after the hearing. "Everything he did was in line with Pancasila."
Pancasila, or five principles, prescribes belief in one God, just and civilised humanity, national unity, democracy through consultations and social justice for all.

The PRD had called for a minimum wage of 7,000 rupiah ($3) a day, withdrawal of political laws, new political parties, a new president, an end to the military's role in social and political affairs and a referendum in East Timor.

Adnan Buyung Nasution, one of Pakpahan's lawyers, said the leader of the unrecognised Indonesian Labour Welfare Union (SBSI) was subjected to a "thought trial" as some of his allegedly subversive acts were academic arguments published in a book.
"The charges are very stretched. If we see the material of the conduct and the statements as grounds for the charges it was all from before July this year," Nasution later told reporters.

"At that time he was not arrested. Only after the July 27 incident was he brought to trial. They cannot prove he was behind the July 27 incident, so they're trying to make accusations on his past conduct and statements," he said.
International labour bodies have said the trial was about the right to organise in Indonesia rather than subversion.
